(CNN) -- Scientists in Colombia have unearthed the remains of a true prehistoric monster believed to be the biggest snake ever to have lived on Earth. An artist's impression of what Titanoboa cerrejonensis would have looked like. Named Titanoboa cerrejonensis, the snake would have weighed 1,140 kilograms (2,500 pounds) and measured 13 meters (42.7 feet) nose to tail tip -- dwarfing the largest modern pythons and anacondas which can grow to 6 meters (19.5 feet). Scientists believe it slithered around the planet between 58 and 60 million years ago. Geologist David Polly, who identified the position of the fossil vertebrae which made a size estimate possible, said in a statement Wednesday: "At its greatest width, the snake would have come up to about your hips. The size is pretty amazing. "But our team went a step further and asked, how warm would the Earth have to be to support a body of this size?" Titanoboa's fossilized remains were discovered at a coal mine in the tropical Cerrejon region of northern Colombia by an international team of scientists. "Truly enormous snakes really spark people's imagination, but reality has exceeded the fantasies of Hollywood," paleontologist Jonathan Bloch, who co-led the expedition, told reporters. "The snake that tried to eat Jennifer Lopez in the movie 'Anaconda' was not as big as the one we found." Based on the snake's size, the team was able to calculate that the mean annual temperature in equatorial South America 60 million years ago would have been about 91 degrees Fahrenheit, about 10 degrees warmer than today, Bloch said. "Tropical ecosystems of South America were surprisingly different 60 million years ago," said Bloch. "It was a rainforest, like today, but it was even hotter and the cold-blooded reptiles were all substantially larger. "The result was, among other things, the largest snakes the world has ever seen...and hopefully ever will." According to Nature.com, snakes are poikilotherms (cold-blooded) that, unlike humans, need heat from their environment to power their metabolism. Therefore research suggests that at the time the region would have had to be no less than 86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit for the snake to have survived. Most large snakes today live in the tropical regions of South America and south-east Asia, where the high temperatures allow them to grow to impressive sizes. Meanwhile, Carlos Jaramillo -- who was also part of the expedition -- said the tropical rainforest at Cerrejon appeared to have thrived at these temperatures. "This data challenges the view that tropical vegetation lives near its climatic optimum, and it has profound implications in understanding the effect of current global warming on tropical plants," he said.

In a remarkable paleontological breakthrough, scientists working in Colombia have uncovered fossilized remains of what is now recognized as the largest snake species to have ever existed on our planet. Named *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*, this colossal serpent has captured the attention of researchers worldwide, offering unprecedented insights into both prehistoric life and ancient climate conditions.

## An Astonishing Scale

The dimensions of Titanoboa are nothing short of staggering. Based on the fossilized vertebrae and other skeletal remains, scientists estimate that this massive snake weighed approximately 1,140 kilograms (roughly 2,500 pounds) and stretched an incredible 13 meters (about 42 feet) in length. To put this into perspective, these measurements dwarf even the largest snakes alive today—modern reticulated pythons and green anacondas, which are already impressive predators in their own right, pale in comparison to this ancient giant. Titanoboa would have been long and heavy enough to overshadow any snake a person might encounter in the modern world, making it a true apex predator of its time.

## The Discovery Site and Timeline

The fossils were unearthed by an international team of researchers at a coal mine located in the Cerrejón region of northern Colombia. This area has proven to be a rich source of paleontological data, preserving remains from a critical period in Earth's history. Based on geological dating, Titanoboa is believed to have lived between 58 and 60 million years ago, placing it firmly in the Paleocene epoch—a time shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs when new ecosystems were rapidly evolving and diversifying to fill ecological niches left vacant.

## A Window into Ancient Climate

Perhaps the most fascinating aspect of this discovery extends beyond the snake itself and into what it reveals about Earth's climatic history. Geologist David Polly and paleontologist Jonathan Bloch collaborated to analyze the significance of Titanoboa's extraordinary size, using it as a proxy to estimate ancient environmental conditions. Their research led them to calculate that equatorial temperatures during this period averaged around 91 degrees Fahrenheit (approximately 33 degrees Celsius)—notably warmer than today's equivalent temperatures by roughly 10 degrees.

This temperature estimation is grounded in a fundamental biological principle: snakes are poikilotherms, meaning they are cold-blooded creatures whose body temperature and, consequently, their metabolic processes and growth potential, are directly influenced by the surrounding environment. Unlike warm-blooded animals that regulate their own body temperature internally, poikilotherms depend heavily on external heat sources to fuel their biological functions. This relationship means that the size a cold-blooded animal can achieve is intrinsically linked to the ambient temperature of its habitat—warmer conditions generally allow for larger body sizes, as increased heat supports more efficient metabolism and growth over the animal's lifetime.

## Implications for Understanding Earth's History

Given this biological relationship, the sheer enormity of Titanoboa serves as compelling evidence that South America's tropical ecosystems were significantly hotter approximately 60 million years ago than they are in the present day. This finding contributes valuable data to our broader understanding of ancient climate patterns and how Earth's temperature has fluctuated over millions of years. The discovery of Titanoboa, therefore, represents far more than simply identifying a record-breaking prehistoric creature—it provides scientists with a unique biological thermometer, offering critical insights into the climatic conditions that shaped ancient ecosystems and the organisms that thrived within them.

In the arid landscape of the Cerrejón coal mine in northeastern Colombia, paleontologists uncovered something extraordinary: fossilized vertebrae so large that researchers initially struggled to believe they belonged to a snake at all. The vertebrae, some measuring several inches across, pointed to a creature of almost unimaginable proportions.

The species, formally named *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*, lived approximately 60 million years ago—just five million years after the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs. The find, first published in the journal *Nature* by a team led by paleontologist Jonathan Bloch, sent shockwaves through the scientific community.

"This wasn't just a big snake," one researcher involved in the initial analysis noted. "This was a snake operating at a completely different scale than anything alive today."

## By the Numbers

Based on the fossilized remains, scientists estimate Titanoboa reached lengths of up to **42 to 45 feet**—roughly the length of a city bus—and weighed an estimated **2,500 pounds**, or more than a small car.

## Comparing Giants: Then and Now

To understand just how extreme Titanoboa's size was, consider its modern relatives:

- **Green Anaconda**: The largest snake alive today typically reaches 17-20 feet and weighs around 550 pounds. Titanoboa was more than twice as long and roughly four to five times heavier.

- **Reticulated Python**: Known as the longest snake species today, some individuals have approached 30 feet—still significantly shorter than Titanoboa.

- **Body Width**: Perhaps most striking, researchers calculated that Titanoboa's body at its thickest point would have been roughly the height of an adult human's waist—meaning the snake could have looked a grown person in the eye while lying flat on the ground.

Unlike modern anacondas and pythons, which are constrictors that ambush prey in water or dense vegetation, Titanoboa likely dominated ancient river systems and swamps, feeding on massive fish and other prey suited to its scale.

## What Snake Size Reveals About Climate

The most significant scientific implication of the discovery lies not in the snake's terrifying dimensions, but in what those dimensions suggest about prehistoric temperatures.

Snakes are ectotherms—commonly known as "cold-blooded" animals—meaning their body temperature and metabolic processes are directly influenced by their environment. Generally, the larger an ectotherm's body size, the warmer its habitat must be to sustain it.

Using this relationship, researchers calculated that for Titanoboa to survive and grow to such an enormous size, the tropical climate of the Paleocene epoch would have needed an average annual temperature between **86 and 93 degrees Fahrenheit**—significantly warmer than the tropics of today, which average around 78 degrees Fahrenheit.

"This tells us that even after the extinction event that killed the dinosaurs, tropical ecosystems were operating in extremely hot conditions," explained one climate scientist familiar with the findings. "Titanoboa essentially serves as a biological thermometer for a period of Earth's history we have limited direct temperature data for."

## Broader Implications for Climate Science

The discovery has become an important data point for scientists studying how ecosystems respond to elevated global temperatures—research with direct relevance to current conversations about modern climate change.

Some key takeaways researchers have drawn:

1. **Tropical regions can sustain higher temperatures than previously modeled**, challenging some assumptions about maximum viable heat thresholds for tropical rainforest ecosystems.

2. **Ectotherm body size serves as a proxy for ancient temperature data**, giving scientists another tool beyond ice cores and sediment analysis to reconstruct historical climate conditions.

3. **Rapid ecosystem recovery after mass extinction was possible**, as the Cerrejón fossil site reveals a thriving, complex rainforest ecosystem just a few million years after the dinosaurs' disappearance—information relevant to understanding biodiversity recovery timelines.

## The Bigger Picture

While Titanoboa's reign ended as global temperatures cooled over millions of years, its fossilized remains continue to offer scientists a rare window into a hotter Earth. As researchers continue to model future climate scenarios, ancient giants like Titanoboa serve as a stark reminder: Earth's climate has swung dramatically before, and the fossil record holds clues about what a significantly warmer planet can produce.
